The fact is, as you've said here, you got out of the JNA by being a malingerer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state once again that I was released from the hospital with a diagnosis where my leg is mentioned. It is true that I added to my nervousness, and if you like, I did not want to serve in the JNA. I could have malingered on any subject, and had I been able to do that, I would have. I would have tricked the Yugoslav People's Army in a worse way than this to avoid doing my military service. But it's not true that I was not nervous, so I'm giving you a precise answer. There's no doubt that I would have used every opportunity to leave the army, to leave that army, but my diagnosis was established medically and it also mentions my leg, because I didn't have to do guard duty or do much foot-walking and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So do you deny what's reported here, the words attributed to you? Do you deny telling this reporter -- do you deny the words attributed to you in this article when you said, I was a malingerer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't deny having said that to the journalist, but I added all this malingering bit so as not to leave the impression -- and so as not to say that there were, in fact, problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So, in other words, you said something that was untrue to the journalist in order to make a better story? Is that a better way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say it was untrue. I just added a bit. So I told the truth, but not the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just want to go a little bit deeper into this article. And if you continue turning the pages of the "Globus" article, General, you're going to see an old photograph of you and some of your childhood class-mates that I thought was worth bringing to everyone's attention. It's on the last page of the original language version, and I'm looking at page 11 of the translation, although, Mr. President, the photo, of course, is not in the translation. This article, General, it has a photograph from your childhood in Siroki Brijeg, and in this photograph we see you together with Mr. Gojko Susak. Do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this, of course, is the same Gojko Susak who was then to go on and serve as the minister of defence for the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So based on the fact, General, that you have virtually no military experience in the JNA, and that you had served in the Croatian Army for only a short time before being elevated to the National Security Council of the Republic of Croatia and to the rank of general in the Croatian Army, what really -- what we can conclude from that is that your very rapid ascension within the Croatian military hierarchy is based upon a personal connection you had with the defence minister of Croatia, Mr. Susak, as opposed to based on any professional experience and qualifications you may have possessed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I had any ambitions like that, Mr. Prosecutor, I would have become the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, not Gojko Susak. Secondly, I'm highly educated in military matters, and I can tell you a lot more than other generals could. I am highly educated in many matters. And in that respect, my promotion and advancement was no quicker than it would otherwise have been normally, given the wartime conditions, because I have a great deal of knowledge. And I can prove that in a hundred different ways. And I was in love with this little girl on the right here all the time. Mirna, her name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your counsel can come back to that in re-direct, if they wish. I'm going to pass over that. General, I want to take you now to your testimony on the 23rd of June in this courtroom. And to start with, I'd ask if the -- I think you have it in your binder, but I'd ask if the technical people could put the map up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you show this photograph taken at the seaside just to see the level of nutrition of people in Herzegovina of this time? Show this photograph of my friend and me. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, your counsel can come back to that one as well. I'd like to move on. As I indicated, I want to talk to you about something you said on the 23rd of June and the map that you brought to court, 3D00543. If we could put 3D00543 in e-court. General, you have it in your binder. It's in the binders that have been distributed as well. And just to remind you, General, this is the map that you testified you made showing the respective positions of the HVO and the ABiH in the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf area on the 12th of January, 1993. Do you recall this map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of June, you testified that this was to prove that the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf took all the dominant heights, completely blocked the passage through Vakuf, rendering it impossible for the brigade commander to get to his headquarters. And you might recall, General, that I actually intervened and asked you to clarify what the green arrow toward the middle of the page was, which indicated the Neretvica Brigade. Do you recall when I intervened because it was pointed out -- or you were asked specifically why no HVO units were indicated as being present on the Makljen Ridge. Do you remember that intervention that I made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, just for starters, the fact that this map doesn't show any HVO presence on Makljen on the 12th of January, 1993, makes the map erroneous, doesn't it? The map is not correct, in that it omits HVO presence at the Makljen Ridge; would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, is that because as you told Judge Antonetti, on the 23rd of June, page 41860 of the transcript, who specifically asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI SAID
utterances.text: "Yes, General, why is it this arrow pointing to Makljen Ridge," he's referring to the Neretvica arrow, "when there is no presence of HVO in Makljen?" And you said: "The HVO was at Makljen, but it's not marked." And then Judge Antonetti said: "There were soldiers in Makljen?" And you answered: "No, not soldiers. There was a check-point, a police check-point, at Makljen. There was no need for these troops to be stationed at Makljen, but cutting Makljen off and taking this check-point would --" I'm sorry, "... taking this check-point in effect would have caused the whole situation in Prozor to fall through." So what you said in response to Judge Antonetti's question on this was that there was, in fact, a check-point, a police check-point, at Makljen. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. At the top of Makljen, there was a police check-point at the ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in fact, there was not only a police check-point, but there were big guns, artillery of the HVO, that it used in this very same period in connection with the Gornji Vakuf operation; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether during the operation, the artillery was brought in, I don't know that, but there was no artillery up at Makljen. There was no need for that, and it wasn't a good position for it. There was no -- it wouldn't have served a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you take a look at the next document, please, P01107. P01107. General, this is an order from your -- well, from Commander Colonel Siljeg, dated 12th of January, the same date as your map, and it's an order. He refers in paragraph 1 to the attack forces of the operative zone, ordering them to route the enemy forces, the BH Army, with the objective of taking control of towns and roads and preventing the enemy from threatening the Croatian population in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. And if you turn to item 3 in this document, page 3 of the English, paragraph 3 pertains to the use of the artillery. And then item 3.4, if you look at that paragraph, General, you'll see at the end that Colonel Siljeg is referring to -- I'll just read the sentence: "Firing position for the T-130 in the Ometala area for the VBR on Makljena and for the PAT and tanks in Prozor." Just so we know, General, what is the VBR that is referred to here? Isn't that a multiple rocket-launcher?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, a multiple-barrel rocket-launcher which is placed either on a truck or is pulled by a truck. And as it says here, quite correctly, this is preparation for an operation. So the VBR will be brought to Makljen, and PATs, tanks to Rama. So he's not even bringing it into combat yet, rather, he is taking it to Prozor. So regardless of the fact that I arrived up there on the 16th, the information that I received was correct, and this testifies to it. So these are preparations for an operation, and the VBR will be brought up to Makljen on a truck or pulled by a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. So to the extent that your map and your testimony indicates there was not or would not have been a multiple rocket-launcher position on Makljen on or after the 12th of January, that's incorrect; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He goes on to say here that it should be -- a VBR should be brought into Makljen and tanks into Rama. Now, whether that was the case on the 12th, that's debatable. I stand by what I said. It might be wrong with respect to a matter of hours or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we then go to the next document, P01162. This is a report of Colonel Siljeg dated 16 January, so this is four days later. Now, on page 2 of the English, at the top, he says: "We began more intense operations on all enemy movements and regrouping." And then skipping down a few lines, he mentions Rama Brigade forces, and he makes reference to 107-millimetre multiple rocket-launcher on Makljen, 120-millimetre mortar from Mount Makljen, and a T-55 battle tank from Makljen. And so, again, General, to the extent your map indicates that there was no HVO presence at Makljen on the 12th of January, isn't that misleading, because, in fact, the HVO had multiple big guns on that feature that it used during the Gornji Vakuf operation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, obviously, yes, because that's when the operation started, but the main feature up on Makljen, which is a hill, is called "Crni Vrh," it's the Crni Vrh feature, 1033. And Siljeg says Crni Vrh has been taken control of, which means that the BH Army forces from the main feature at Crni Vrh were in control of Makljen. And the HVO, before the start, only had a point up there or, rather, a police check-point; whereas once the operation was launched, then that's normal, bringing these in. And that's how Crni Vrh was taken, obviously. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is P01183. This is from Commander Siljeg on the 18th of January, where he says, and I'm looking at the second line of the text, he says: "We hereby inform you that given that this morning we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, there is heavy fighting going on over there ..." So again, General, to the extent that your map and your testimony indicated that there was no HVO position or military presence at Makljen during this period of time, that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's quite the reverse; what I said is completely correct. Because if the BH Army, and the previous document said that, was not in control of Crni Vrh, Makljen, why, then, was fierce fighting going on there? If the HVO previously controlled Makljen and Crni Vrh, then there would not be fierce fighting going on there. So what I said, my statement is correct, and it's correct that the HVO was not up at Makljen, which is a hill, the main feature, but that it was taken over by the BH Army, and that's why the operation started, because it had its positions up there, and it had complete control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I remember having asked this question, and at the time I wanted to ask you some questions on Makljen because we had heard about it. Why is it that on this map -- and in fact it would have been useful for you to tell us that the position of the HVO and BiH were there at a specific date, you should have pointed out the day, but I would like to know why you did not mark this map and stated that the HVO was there after Crni Vrh was taken. It's the hill that is above Makljen. Why did you not mention it? Is that because the map has been drafted or has been drawn after the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, the map was drawn up on the basis of documents subsequently, the documents that I had in the Detention Unit, and on the basis of consultations. Secondly, the map was confirmed by a major of the British Army. And, thirdly, you would have to draw a new map for every single day. Well, not only day; military maps change from one hour to the next. So this is the initial starting position for which I claimed, on the basis of talks I had and so on, that the cause of the beginning of the HVO action was to pull out of an encirclement. That was the initial point. Now, later on, subsequently, the fact that VBRs were brought in and tanks, you have to follow the situation from one hour to the next, and you ought to bring in Siljeg to tell you how the situation evolved over the days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in military terms, if I understand you correctly, in Makljen the HVO was controlling traffic, there were check-points, and on the next hill in Crni Vrh there was the presence of the ABiH, and you attacked this position and actually captured it. Is this what happened, militarily-wise, after which, of course, you controlled Makljen as well as the other elevation that had been previously held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is what the document says, orders that this elevation at 1.300 metres was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'll let you go on, because you may be asking the question that I would have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have one more document on this point, Judge Trechsel, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My document -- my question refers to this document. Mr. Stringer has put this to you and then said, Doesn't this show that the Makljen was in possession and held by the HVO with heavy weapons? And you have then answered that this was not so; on the contrary, quite the reverse. Page 66, line 3, following. And you say, line 5: "Then was fierce fighting going on there." And you refer this "there" to Crni Vrh and Makljen. Now, if I look at the text that I have in an English translation, which, of course, may not be correct, I read it differently. In the text, Colonel Siljeg says: "This morning, we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen. There is heavy fighting ongoing over there, and therefore we cannot perform the evacuation." In my reading, "there" does not refer to Makljen, where there is nothing to evacuate, anyway, but to Gornji Vakuf. And so I think it's not at all what you told us, but what Mr. Stringer suggested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The evacuation of the wounded was supposed to take place from Bugojno, and it has nothing to do with this. This -- well, Siljeg is writing to the brigade in Bugojno, saying, We cannot -- or, rather, You cannot, because of the fighting, take the wounded which were usually transported to Croatia via that road, you cannot evacuate them. The wounded in Bugojno are the result of the fighting between the BH Army and the HVO, on the one side, and the Serbs. Bugojno is at peace. There's still fighting only the with the Serbs. There are wounded, and they are being taken away. But here the fighting started. There is no military reason -- Serb lines were 20 kilometres. The BH Army did not have any military reason to be on Makljen or Crni Vrh, which is a dominant height. Well, yeah, okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's not the question at all. You pretend that "heavy fighting" refers to Makljen. I read this document as saying that heavy fighting occurred in Gornji Vakuf, which was under attack by the HVO, as Colonel Siljeg says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of translation you get. You go to Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, and this is where there is fierce fighting. There's fierce fighting at Makljen. I don't know if the translation is bad or you cannot get the clarity of it all, but there is fighting at Makljen, because the BH Army controls Crni Vrh and everything in Vakuf. And it is important to note here that Siljeg says the greens, that's the term for the Muslims, You in Bugojno should keep calm and try to convince them that nothing should happen. Well, at any rate, I still stand by the map, and the testimony, and everything I said about Gornji Vakuf, and I'm ready to provide additional explanations as you ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think it is done with document, but regarding the possibility of wrong or -- yes, wrong and maybe -- wrong translation, and maybe that was the reason of confusion, when you read -- first of all, the translation is unrevised, so it is not yet confirmed, really. And when you read, in second and third line that: "This morning we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, there is heavy fighting ongoing over there ..." I think that more correct translation would be: "We have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, where heavy fighting is going on ..." But perhaps somebody should read the entire document in Croatian. So I'm not telling you it's entirely wrong, but it is not very precise, and it might allow different interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you please read the first two sentences on the -- or the first -- actually, it's one sentence, the first sentence of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the original document -- Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I quote: "On the basis of your report, in which you demand an evacuation of the wounded from Bugojno, we hereby inform you that since this morning we have been in the throes of an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, where there is heavy fighting, and the evacuation cannot be carried out." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. As I see military activities, when you attack point B from point A, then the heavy fighting is on point B. If point A is under heavy attack, which is necessary that there is fighting, you will not start an attack. But I leave it at that. I just want you to know that I do not find your answer convincing, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, this last document, if we understand the document well, there is a request to evacuate wounded people from Bugojno. And Colonel Siljeg is answering, saying that it is absolutely impossible to proceed for the following reason: Because we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from Makljen. This is what he is answering. Now, if you connect this document with the previous document we saw earlier, when Crni is being captured, if I understand well, before Gornji Vakuf, then there would have been an attack of the other position held by the ABiH in Crni Vrh, and Gornji Vakuf would have been attacked at a later stage secondly, or were the two attacks simultaneous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the elevations that were taken by the BH Army were attacked simultaneously, the elevations taken to control the HVO in Gornji Vakuf. So first Crni Vrh, and Crni Vrh is far from Vakuf. It takes a while. One needs to fight for a long time between Crni Vrh and Vakuf. Perhaps my answers are not very convincing, but your military knowledge, Judge Trechsel, is highly debatable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, please don't talk about the competence of Judges regarding military matters, because they could prove you wrong. Now, what I would like to say, but it's not in the English version, you said, We attacked Crni first. Is this what happened, you attacked Crni first? In the French interpretation, I heard "we first attacked Crni."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Siljeg launched the attack in the direction of Crni Vrh, not from Crni Vrh. You have to take Crni Vrh and then the next elevation, the next elevation, based on the disposition of their units and as the units retreated. It's a war. There's a dynamics of movement. It depends on whether somebody fled, is fighting back, or surrendered to you. Likewise, the dominant heights that the BH Army held in Vakuf were also under attack. The repeater -- well, they had taken everything. The map is crystal clear, the situation. And then as days went by, the fighting progressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. In terms of military warfare, did the attack start from Makljen? This is what Mr. Stringer was trying to highlight. Did everything start from Makljen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's obvious that there were other attacks before the 18th. Attacks were launched on some other elevations, but this one was launched on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, will you please look at the preceding document, 1162. I have, of course, only the English version, and there what I would like to refer to is on the second page, but it starts with reference to Mount Crni Vrh. It's the first page in the Croatian document. And two days before the document we have now been talking about, we have this report which says, Mount Crni Vrh was taken, which was an important stronghold. So what makes you tell us that two days later, there is still an attack on Crni Vrh going on? This does not hold water, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, Crni Vrh is about 15 kilometres from Vakuf as the crow flies, and probably there was a counter-attack. And 15 kilometres, well, that's not the only elevation. They have a whole series. Now is starting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please spare us your fantasy of, "probably this was or that was" hypothesis. Nothing like that is borne out from the document. But I will give back to Mr. Stringer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before Mr. Stringer can actually take the floor, I would like to move to private session because the Trial Chamber has something to announce. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we're in open session. Mr. Praljak, earlier I told you that you were going to have to answer questions, and it's because I knew that you were going to be in the hot seat and you were going to react. Let me tell you that my fellow Judges, myself, everyone asking questions to you, really want to know what happened. You've seen that sometimes documents are ambiguous, sometimes there are documents that are difficult to understand, which is why we put questions. Here we're talking about military matters, and we're trying to understand what went on. Some might have the same competence as you, some might have less, some might have more, but that's not the problem. We're trying to intelligently understand what is written in all these documents. According to the Prosecution, an attack was launched on Gornji Vakuf, and we're trying to place the forces on the field as they were. Earlier, my fellow Judge was trying to understand how far Makljen was from Gornji Vakuf. We have to know this. You just told us that it's about 15 kilometres away. Very well; if you say so. If the Prosecutor doesn't agree with you, he'll say, No, it's not 15; it's 5, or 10, or whatever. We'll see. But please, stay cool. Keep your cool. This is the very beginning. And we're just talking about Gornji Vakuf. Myself, just like my fellow Judges, like everyone here in this room, is trying to understand whether the HVO attacked, whether the ABiH attacked. Your case, up until now, was that it was the ABiH that attacked first. And now, using the military documents, we're trying to check whether this case holds water or not. Do you understand this? And we need your active participation. We need you to answer the questions. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you are a supreme French diplomat, in addition to being a marvellous judge, but that's not what this is all about. First of all, when you come to things like this, the map was kept here for a minute, and then we proceeded to discuss without the map and to get to a solution. If you want to talk about military issues, we should have a big map here, I should be in a position to make markings on the map, we should have five maps, so that -- well, of course, based on the documents, I could then tell you how the situation evolved on the basis of my knowledge. Secondly, without getting embroiled in legal matters, I know full well the depth of my ignorance here, but I know also things that I know. His Honour Judge Trechsel cannot tell me twice and expect me not to respond, and give me his arguments about how a military action proceeded and then to tell me that I'm not telling the truth, that I'm lying, and that this is not in line with the documents. Well, it doesn't work with me. To put it quite simply, it doesn't work. I really have a high regard for Judge Trechsel, and if he were to fall into the river tomorrow, I would leap in and save him, as I have done several times. But when it comes to my principles, my testimony, and my life, there is no compromise, there can be no compromise. I will answer the questions, and I would like to be given two maps here of the area around Gornji Vakuf and to bring back the map that we had before so that we can see where the BH Army units were deployed. The problem, Judge Antonetti, is quite clear, Your Honour. An English major testified here that the BH Army put a noose around the HVO's neck in and around the town of Vakuf. No army can bear that, and this is why an attack was launched on the elevations, the attack which I stopped on the 23rd and the troops did not enter Vakuf. These are the facts, and now questions, details -- every detail, every question, I will deal with it, but this game of cat and mouse, attack on A and then B, well, Slobodan Praljak is not the one to stand for it. Clinton, Obama, and even if God himself came here, I would say, No, Lord, I do not agree with you. And when it comes to everything else, finding the truth here, I do not respect any authority in advance. You will sign the judgement under your authority at the end. It is your right and it gives you power. But until that time there is only the authority of logic. I’m just telling the truth here to the best of my knowledge. I'm here to tell the truth, and when the logic is all wrong, it's skewed, then I want to say it. Believe me, Your Honours, with full respect to you, as persons -- well, this is a case in logic, methodology, epistemology, there are things that I know, and I will not keep silent. I will answer any question, I will admit to malingering, I will admit to everything, apart from those things that are simply not true. And could we please have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not about merits of the case, but this is an unpleasant situation, and I might help to solve it. I am from that area. When we say "Makljen," we mean the ridge between the two mountains. Makljen is also a fairly big mountain, and in this document, which was quoted by Judge Trechsel a moment ago, two lines above what he quoted, it is stated that shots were fired from Makljen on Crni Vrh, and then it goes on to say that a T-55 - it's probably a tank - fired on Crni Vrh from Makljen. And Crni Vrh, the way I understand it, is the highest -- it's the summit of the Makljen Mountain. So it's the same as if you were to say somebody took Mont Blanc, and that means that they took the Alps. I'm just trying to help you all get some knowledge of the situation. I'm not talking about the operations, because I don't know much about that, but I do know about the lay of the land. And if I helped you in the situation, then the purpose of my intervention has been fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Shortly, mainly a correction to the transcript on page 73, line 24, we read: "There is 50 kilometres between Crni Vrh and Gornji Vakuf." I think it ought to read "15," not "50."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the assistance of Mr. Prlic. I was referring to the next line, actually, where it simply says: "Mount Crni Vrh was taken." Now, maybe there are other understandings, and I read it in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak asked for a break, and I think we need a break, so we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for giving me the floor. Following this whole discussion that we had, I went back to the transcript just to reassure myself - page 73, lines 7 through 9. Judge Trechsel literally said, I'll quote in English, just to make sure there's no confusion, that was recorded: [In English] "Spare us your fantasy of -- probably this was -- that was a hypothesis ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth, another sentence that I believe has nothing to do with this. What I'm trying to say here is the use of this word that Judge Trechsel used, vis a vis the accused, after the accused, in a previous answer, stated nothing but two facts about mileage, so this is in no way something that can be termed anyone's fantasy. Given the nature of the reaction that this received, I can only say that I can understand the statement in the following way. It actually expresses a certain position and a certain conviction on the part of the Judge, the position or the conviction that was put forward during a trial. This might be an indicator of prejudice in terms of the conclusions being made. Any sensible person could have read it this way. We don't even need to talk. I have arrived at my conclusion, everything else is fantasy. I will give it some serious thought, whether I can perhaps ask for Judge Trechsel to step down from the Chamber. I do believe that a Judge who is part of the Chamber should not be allowed to address the accused in this way before the OTP's cross has even begun. Perhaps this was a piece of awkward phrasing by the Judge. Maybe it was a bit too emotional. I'm not going into that. Perhaps the Judge can explain. Nevertheless, the way it looks now on the transcript really seems like someone is jumping to conclusions there and as if the Judge already had his own solution made up in his head. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic, for giving me an opportunity to comment. I would concede that the wording is perhaps not very well chosen, absolutely, but I want to make it clear that this refers to line 5, where

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK SAID
utterances.text: "Probably there was a counter-attack." The facts were that we have a report of the 16th where Colonel Siljeg reports, We have taken Crni Vrh. And two days later he reports from Makljen, We attack Gornji Vakuf. Then Mr. Praljak said that the heavy fighting, of which the colonel also wrote in his text, that this was probably at Makljen because, always what Mr. Praljak said, they were fighting to, first of all, free Crni Vrh. Now, as we have a document in which Colonel Siljeg reports two days earlier that he has taken Crni Vrh, and no document whatsoever which would suggest that there had been a counter-attack, this reply from Mr. Praljak, I think, can be called a fantasy or, as I have added, a hypothesis. It is a hypothesis; however, it is not supported by the document. That is all which I mentioned, and I find it difficult to regard this as depicting any form of bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for this explanation, Your Honour. Perhaps that constitutes a sufficient clarification. I'm not sure I understand fully. Nevertheless, the fact remains, the way your remark was phrased, "Please spare us your fantasy," objectively it caused those present to feel the way I have just described, and that is no fantasy, because we are talking about facts derived from documents, which can in no way be described as fantasy. As for those documents, if you allow, each of us present here can choose to read them in a different way. Just by way of an example, the whole discussion was triggered by 3D00543. Questions were asked that were not entirely in keeping with what we see on the map, and the discussion followed from that. Mr. Praljak tried to say just that. As a matter of fact, at no point in time did he manage to finish saying everything that he wanted to say. The map is dated the 12th of January, and as he told us when he first presented this map himself and, in part, explained today, it was drawn based on such documents as were available in detention. This is an attempt to display facts based on a number of different documents. The snake-like arrow pointing towards the Makljen Pass, the lowest one, the southern-most one in the map, if you like, is also a fact derived from a document, an army document, showing that the army was planning to move in that direction, or that was my understanding. Had all of that been clarified properly, we'd all been privy to all the details and probably none of this would have come to pass. The point, however, is this: One must have patience. We are all aware of the fact that we are dealing with an enormous amount of documents. These three documents do not give us the whole picture. We know that. We've heard evidence to that effect, and we're about to hear more. Therefore, I'm afraid that this might be an indication of a premature conclusion, because we've not heard a witness on this yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the document that we see on our screens, P01162, the item that reads: "Crni Vrh has been taken," right underneath it reads: "Enemy forces attempting a breakthrough towards our unit's or our force's positions were fired at and repelled in a vigorous way." They did take Crni Vrh, which is some 15 kilometres from Vakuf as the crow flies, but here the BH Army attempted yet another breakthrough to approach those forces that were there. Sniper fire killed two scouts from the Rama Brigade, two of those men who were reconnoitering the area to see if there were any enemy forces ahead. We should take this hour by hour and fact by fact. Unfortunately, it's not possible to just simplify this altogether and explain a complex military operation, with all its details, in just a couple of words. Nevertheless, it reads, Well, the fact that Crni Vrh was taken does not mean that much, because this was followed immediately by a small-scale counter-strike by the enemy, if we can call it that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic wants to take the floor. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. A technical matter. When we say "Crni Vrh," Your Honours, I think you said that you were at Makljen, that you visited Makljen. If you face Prozor from Makljen, Crni Vrh is the one to your left, the distance being about 7 or 8 kilometres. 1303 is one of many trig points at Crni Vrh. You can fight around Crni Vrh for a whole day without taking Crni Vrh in its entirety. This is a single trig point in Crni Vrh. It's a large mountain that stretches for, I think, between 7 or 10 kilometres. It starts at Karamustafici in Vakuf and stretches all the way towards the south-east. You were at Makljen, and looking towards Prozor, Crni Vrh was probably on your left. That is the large mountain. 1300 is a single trig point, a single elevation there, technically speaking. You can actually see that on the map. There are five or six references on that map, Crni Vrh, Crni Vrh, Crni Vrh. It's a whole mountain starting near Vakuf and extending towards the south-east. So much for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General Petkovic, for this clarification regarding the elevation. There is, indeed, an elevation 1303, and there could be other elevations in one single mountain. I would like to go back to what Counsel Kovacic just said. I think, Counsel Kovacic, that you have to make a distinction between facts and the responsibility of the accused. I believe that a Judge can say to an accused, You said this and that, and I don't agree with that and that, without having to draw immediately conclusions as to the responsibility of an accused. I personally asked questions to Mr. Praljak because sometimes I don't agree with him, sometimes I said to him or I made him understand such. So we may disagree on a point, and in this very instance the accused can understand that a Judge disagree, and it is the accused's duty to make sure that the Judge understands that he's making a mistake; hence, the need to take the stand as an accused. So I wanted to clarify this, because you have to make a distinction between the position of a Judge on facts and a position of a Judge in terms of criminal responsibility, which is not at all the same thing. A Judge is perfectly in a position to draw a conclusion on a fact and say, As far as I can see on the map that General Praljak has showed us, it's 1.300 metres. And then we can say that the witness can say, There is a mistake, that is an elevation, but there are other elevations within the same mountain, without assuming that the Judge has drawn the conclusions that all accused are guilty. This is the distinction that we have to make. So, Mr. Praljak, once again, when you feel that Judges do not share your point of view, you keep your cool and you try and prove otherwise. This is the whole point of an adversarial procedure. And the fact that you are taking the stand means that we are going to have more information about this case. So when you see that through Judges' questions, they are going into one direction, and, according to you, you feel that it's the wrong direction, you should very calmly say, Well, you said this and that, but according to this and that document, it's not the case, and you can tell the truth. Mr. Springer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I'm a passionate person, and so is Judge Trechsel, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The President's given me the floor, and I'm not, at the very beginning of this cross-examination, going allow the general to do what he's done so many times before with the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You'll come back to that, General Praljak. I have given Mr. Stringer the floor, so he's going to ask you questions. Please, Mr. Stringer, ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this is not the Gornji Vakuf part of the cross-examination. We're going to come back to it at a later time. I'm, at this stage, focusing on specific things that you've said at various times of your testimony. And for the moment I'm focusing on this one aspect of your testimony that related to Gornji Vakuf concerning this map and the testimony that you gave us indicating that on the 12th of January, 1993, the only presence of the HVO, in your testimony, was the police check-point on Makljen. Okay, that's the point I'm focusing on. Now, I've shown you a series of documents, starting from the 12th of January and extending for a few days after, indicating that, in fact, the HVO had artillery pieces, multiple rocket-launchers, at the Makljen feature which it used to launch an attack on Gornji Vakuf. Now, just to tie this off, I want to take you to one more document, and then, hopefully, we can round this off. It's the next document in your binder. It's P01214. I think it's the document actually that your counsel, Mr. Kovacic, made a reference to a few moments ago. This is dated the 19th of January, 1993. It's a communication to the Command of the 4th Corps, reporting on the situation in Gornji Vakuf. This is obviously -- I say the 4th Corps. This is the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what it said here is that: "The situation in Gornji Vakuf is very complex. The attack of the HVO units on this city is carried out from the direction of Prozor, from the area of Makljen Pass." And it goes on to say that: "The city and our city defenders are under fire from all artillery weapons...," et cetera. And then - and this is something I think you referred to in your testimony - this order, then, in paragraph 1 directs that the Neretvica Brigade and adequate forces from Prozor are to be engaged in taking over Makljen, and to hold that pass. All right? Now, is it correct, then, that on the map you brought to the courtroom, showed to the Judges, the green arrow here in the centre, the squiggly arrow, and the indication "Neretvica" there, is a reference to the operation of the ABiH that was carried out pursuant to this order to take the Makljen feature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And so this is from the 19th of January, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what you've done here, General, is to include here -- well, let me put it this way: Would you agree with me, sir, that it would not be necessary for the ABiH to deploy the entire Neretvica Brigade and other adequate forces from Prozor if the only thing that they had to take on the Makljen feature was an HVO police check-point?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have engaged the HVO forces. They should have reached the pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: First of all, I've been told that the transcript doesn't indicate the general's answer to my last couple of questions, so let me ask those to you again, General. This is looking at your map, 3D00543. The wavy green line is a reference to the operation of the Neretvica Brigade, is that correct, that was carried out pursuant to the order which is P01214?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The road taken by the Neretvica Brigade to get there and what it was supposed to do was drawn based on that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what you've done on this map is actually to reflect events not just from the 12th of January, but also one week later, on the 19th of January, where you've indicated the operation of the Neretvica Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, the positions were marked, as well as what the Neretvica Brigade was supposed to get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But, of course, what you didn't do, General, and what makes this so misleading, and which makes your testimony so misleading, is the fact that you omitted to include on the map all of the HVO artillery and guns that were on the Makljen feature from this period between the 12th of January to the 19th; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, no maps were drawn showing the actions after the 12th. One was drawn in relation to the 12th and based on this order marking the direction of the Neretvica Brigade's deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the arrow marking the direction of the Neretvica Brigade's deployment reflects events taking place one week later on the 19th; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what's missing here and which you would agree with me is vitally important to understanding is the fact that what's missing is all of the HVO big guns that were on the Makljen feature which gave rise to the need for the Neretvica Brigade to go there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO did not have big guns. They were relatively small guns. It's true that the Neretvica Brigade was thrown into action once the combat was already underway, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you told Judge Antonetti, in response to his question, that the only thing the HVO had on Makljen was an HVO police check-point, when you were describing the content of this map that you produced, that wasn't correct, that wasn't true, because you omitted to tell us about the HVO artillery that was on that position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, sir. I said specifically that when the HVO operation began, the guns were brought in. It was sent to Prozor, a certain number, and then a grenade launcher was also deployed at Makljen. You have a time continuum here. On the 12th, there is no HVO artillery there. Siljeg is only introducing it. The map in relation to the 12th, the only inaccuracy it shows is the snake-like arrow showing the introduction of Neretvica. For the sake of precision, there should have been a remark there that read the 19th of January. That is the only error. Everything else is accurate. But if you can't draw ten maps, you have me here to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue with you about it. But isn't it more correct to say that for the sake of precision, if you're going to make a reference to the Neretvica operation of the 19th of January, you also need to include the positions of the HVO artillery that were on the Makljen feature at that time, the 19th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that would be your task. You have to prove an HVO attack. You should be producing 20 maps with a timeline to each of them, and then I would answer your questions. As in many other cases, the position I'm facing here is that you haven't done your job properly. You simply write something up, and it is up to us to defend ourselves by proving our innocence. Draw all those maps based on documents, accurate maps, hour by hour, day by day, instead of me having to draw maps for you based on some general statements that you are making, in order to prove my innocence. You are turning the tables around here, and it's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You brought this map, you gave it to the Judges. You took it upon yourself to do that. Now, the fact is - and I'm going to come back to my question from previous - to be more precise and to be more accurate, you should have indicated the position of the HVO guns on Makljen on the 19th of January. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, I could do that, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do it yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have a document on the screen and it comes from the enemy, from the 4th Corps, sent to Pasalic by the Supreme Command of the ABiH. In this document, there is a description of the situation, from their side, of course, on January 19, 1993. First point, the situation in Gornji Vakuf is very complex; no one can deny this. Then they say there's an attack of the HVO units from Makljen. We all agree on that also. Then there is no attack of infantry yet. However, he says that the city is under artillery fire, but I believe that in terms of facts, it's the rest that's more important. He is saying that HVO forces come from Tomislavgrad, Livno, and other cities from Herzegovina. That's what it said in this document. Then there is the order, obviously, to do something about the situation. There is an order given to the Neretvica Brigade to engage its forces. This is a very important document, you know, as far as -- when it comes to knowing who attacked first, whether it's the HVO or the ABiH. When reading this document, in terms of facts, any reasonable trier of fact might infer or could infer that it's the HVO that attacked because they brought troops from Tomislavgrad, Livno, and other towns in Herzegovina that captured the Crni Hill, placed its artillery, and is starting to shell the city. Now, what can you say about this? What can you say about the fact that using this -- by reading this document, it does look like it's the HVO who started attacking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on documents that are exhibits before this Chamber, I drew this map in relation to that particular date. The Neretvica bit was not added. What is true beyond a shadow of a doubt is that the HVO's intention was to, by attacking -- and in military terminology, this is called active defence, and that must be reflected on the record. The HVO attacks the BH Army in the sense of active defence, because the BH Army is a friendly army which takes all the elevations in and around Gornji Vakuf, leaving the HVO in the same situation that it left the HVO in, in Konjic and Bugojno later on, pulling the rug from under its feet and hanging it to dry. Militarily, that is something that one cannot allow. The VRS lines were 20 kilometres to the west, as the crow flies. It is not disputed that the HVO is attacking. But now we're all calm here, and, for example, someone from the Defence or the Prosecutor starts bringing in machine-guns, saying, Don't mind me, just you go on with your discussion. And then one of the accused brings another machine-gun, and you start wondering, what's going on here? If a brigade commander of a friendly army cannot reach his own command without being escorted by UNPROFOR, we know by this time that we are facing an aggressor army sealing off all communication towards Central Bosnia and surrounding HVO on all sides, without defending their lines facing the VRS. That is why the HVO is attacking. I shall say this time and again. There is no dispute about this. The HVO is attacking because it is defending. There is something called "defence." Right or wrong? The Americans are attacking Iraq because they say they are defending from biochemical weapons. It's just that we were entirely in the right, and I don't know about Iraq, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, at least with my question, you're now saying that you're not contesting the fact that the HVO attacked. But of course you're saying that it was in the framework of a defence operation, but it's still an attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, active defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to skip a couple of documents that are in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, on the 5th of May, do you remember giving this testimony about snipers, page 39581 of the transcript, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, last time you told us that you would proceed according -- along topics, different topics. I forgot to ask you what the first topic was. Credibility, was that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think you could put it that way, Mr. President. It's a collection of items taken from specific pieces of evidence that the general gave during his direct or during the cross of someone else, and there are a few more related to this, going to prior testimony and credibility. And then after that, we're going to move into some other more substantive topics, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, on the 5th of May, 2009, you said: "Secondly, never during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO did I ever receive information from anyone about the existence of any sniper nest whatsoever. Now, the fact that people sitting in APCs heard shooting and then said they were fired at by snipers, that goes against the grain of logic, because if you're in an APC, you can't hear very much." So do you remember that testimony, denying knowing anything about any sniper nests? That would have been on the 5th of May, so it was the second day of your testimony, now quite some time ago.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Mostar, as far as Mostar is concerned? That referred to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, I don't know. I mean, what you said here is: "Never during the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO ..." So that implies something that's broader than Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it was related to Mostar. I remember very well. I said that if there was the assertion that there were some sniper nests in the town of Mostar, either of the BH Army or through UNPROFOR mediation, I never received any report on the existence of any such sniper nest which would shoot at civilians and the rest. That's what I said, and that is what is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, then, is it correct that you do not deny that the HVO equipped sniper units and that you deployed those sniper units within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As every other army, the HVO had sniper rifles and people in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. If you'll turn to the next document, it's P03912, and just to confirm what you've said, General. I don't think it's necessarily controversial. This is an order by a gentleman with the 2nd HVO Brigade, and he makes reference to a verbal order of Major General Slobodan Praljak. It's dated the 3rd of August, 1993, in which he's ordering that members of the sniper squad of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO in Mostar, and then he gives the names of those individuals, that those -- that that sniper squad is to report immediately to you in Prozor, and that this order then is to serve as a pass for all the check-points. So, General, isn't it true that the HVO did, in fact, have at least one sniper unit in Mostar, as part of the 2nd Brigade, in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then do you recall this specific event where you directed that those -- the sniper squad was to leave Mostar and come report to you in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny that, but from this perspective I really can't remember that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again related to snipers in Mostar, could you turn, please, to the next document, P03351. And, General, I'll point out to you that because this document is dated the 10th of July, 1993, it's from the period prior to the time you took command of the HVO Main Staff. This is a report on the work of the Defence Department, and so this document, I believe, is one emanating from the office of Mr. Stojic. I'm going to direct you to page 9 of the English version, page 7 of your version, the bottom quarter of the English version. I'll read you some -- I'll read a little bit of text, General, and then tell me when you've found it. It says: "At our request, training was organised for snipers because an evident problem in Mostar was that the other side that exceptionally good snipers which, in fact, thwarted the operations of our units." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "Six pairs of snipers were trained, and at the end of the course their results were up to five times better than when they first began training. Among the problems encountered during the course was the lack of weapons of sufficient quality and the lack of time, as this is a very complex subject. All the trainees were exceptionally satisfied, and now the score of sniper battles in Mostar is up to six to one in our favour." So, General, at a later point in the cross-examination, we're going to talk about the situation in Mostar, specifically as regards snipers. But just for our purposes here I wanted to clarify, at the very least, your testimony, that you had no information from anyone about the existence of any sniper nest whatsoever. Now, in fact, General, based on what you've said and what's indicated in this document, the HVO did possess snipers that it deployed in Mostar and elsewhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this document and according to what I know, the HVO did have snipers. When I was referring to sniper nests, I was referring to those sniper nests for which it was claimed they shot at civilians, on the basis of the papers brought in by the expert witness, and I stated my views on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to talk about the targeting issue later, but I wanted to clarify, at least for now, the existence of snipers within the HVO, based on the one bit of testimony that I directed you to. So we'll come back to this. The next item I have, General, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, still regarding facts, this document on snipers is quite important because it does reveal that the HVO had snipers. I'm looking at the date, July 10th, 1993. Now, when looking at the document read by Mr. Stringer, Mr. Stringer, who read this last paragraph, they said that on the other side, that's the ABiH, I guess, maybe also the Serbs, but it's not really clear. It says that on the other side, they have exceptionally good snipers, so -- and the HVO is lacking in this respect. So six pairs of snipers, does that mean twelve snipers? Twelve snipers, six pair of snipers? Yes. Twelve snipers are going to be trained, and then the ratio is going to be switched over, because after training, the ratio is 6:1 in favour of the HVO now. So first consequence regarding facts: Any Judge would like to know whether the HVO had snipers before July 10th, whether these snipers were trained as of July 10th. If the HVO had no sniper before July 10th, then all those killed before July 10th can't be blamed on the HVO because, by definition, the HVO would have had no snipers. But then after July 10th, all those killed, well, there's a mathematical probability that they might have been killed by the HVO snipers who were well trained, as we see here. What's your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. What I can say is that while I was commander, snipers did exist, that they were trained ones, that they had gone through training, which also meant that they were taught who they had the right to fire at and why, that is to say, to shoot enemy soldiers, and here they claim that this Skoko who was killed came in 61, HVO 61. We saw documents showing that a number of English citizens, some of them members of previous English armies, were in the HVO, and I sent them packing from the HVO, and then they joined up with the BH Army. And we saw a document whereby they were paid. One of them was exceptionally good, and he was able to kill HVO soldiers even through little gaps of this size. He could wait for hours, see in the dark, and Santic's men told me how very skilled and dangerous he was. So that's all I can say. Snipers did exist, but I was speaking about sniper nests and civilians, and I've said all that before. I was never informed about that in any way, that that was being done, and I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, two -- excuse me, Mr. Stringer. Two questions. The first, a very easy one that can shortly be answered. When you took over with the HVO, did you read this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second question, perhaps you can help me understand, because I do not quite understand the meaning of the mentioning here that, I quote from the English text, of course: "Now the score of sniper battles in Mostar is up to 6:1 in our favour." What does this mean, "the score of sniper battles"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly, Judge Trechsel, the sniper is used to eliminate the adversary's sniper. That's what happens most often. And this report claims that the HVO snipers killed six times more of their combatants and snipers than they were able to kill ours. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer, again to disturb you and not to allow you to speak, but it is a follow-up question of mine about the snipers, and also referring to the President's previous question about the dates. When he said that July the 10th is a kind of dividing line concerning the sniper's activity, I would like only to say that according to the title of the report on page 1 in the English version, I believe that is of the English, anyway, that it is a report on the work of the Defence Department for the January-June 1993 period, end of the quotation, and therefore I believe that July the 10th is not -- of course, this report is dated July the 10th. On the other hand, the report speaks about the six months before, that is, January-June. So my question is that: What is in the report, you mentioned that you didn't read the report at that time, but, anyway, you have it before you, that those subject matters which are being read in the report, they are -- they are meant to cover the period of the first year -- sorry, first half a year of 1993. So my question is that it is your understanding as well, what I am saying, that it is a report on the first year of -- first half year of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, this is correct, but the fighting in Mostar started on the 30th of June, and in all likelihood the snipers on both sides started operating on the 30th of June, 1993, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to intervene because this might cause some confusion. If we look at how this document is marked in e-court, it's marked as a military police report on the work for the first part of 1993, so the Prosecution described this as a report on the work of the military police and not of the Defence Department. If you look at the document that we have in our hands, we will see that on the first page, it says: "The report on the work of the Defence Department," but if you look at the contents of the document from page 1 to the last page, it pertains to the military police, at least the way we have it printed out. I didn't have time to go through all of it in e-court. So this is a report of the military police, so lest there be some confusion, the witness responding on something that does not have to do with the military element of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we've referred to the title of the document as it appears. No one's saying that the title is incorrect. I think we can all read and determine for ourselves, you know, whether it relates to a specific part of the Defence Department or not. Judge Prandler actually anticipated one of the clarifications I was going to seek, which was that this report pertains to the period of January to June of 1993, which would suggest that the training of the snipers that's referred to in this report would have taken place at some time during that period, but we don't -- we don't know when. I'd be really grateful if I could just try to continue my cross-examination without so much intervention. It's extremely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured, Mr. Stringer, when Judges put questions, it's not deducted from your time. You will have your 40 hours, all of them. No risk to that. But Ms. Alaburic did raise a problem. Look at the report in the B/C/S version. There's a first page, cover page. It's the report from the Department of -- report on the Department of Defence for the first semester of 1993, as my fellow Judge Prandler said. Now take a look at the second page in B/C/S, and there it starts at point 2.33. So obviously there are other pages, but they're missing. The report, in English, translated into English, might hint at the fact that it's a direct report, but what we have here is not a full report. We only have excerpts of this report. The previous pages are missing. Do you agree with this, Mr. Stringer? It's not a full report that we have; it's only a partial report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It appears we have what I'd call a part of chapter 2. It clearly begins with section 2, and so that implies that there's a section 1 somewhere. I think -- I was just saying to my colleague, Ms. Moe, that I believe that this is a part of a larger Defence Department report that has chapters from all the various departments, and we can look for that or clarify that over the break -- or over the weekend, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, you have the entire weekend to do that, because I think it's time to finish, Mr. Stringer, at least for this week. Actually, it's almost quarter to, and we're going to adjourn, come back -- I'm sure you have other binders than this one, right, Mr. Stringer? But you only give us the first one; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what's happening, Mr. President, is I indicated a couple of weeks ago that we're trying to -- in order to assemble them in the order that they'll be referred to, it's a continuing process. And I should also say that because we're only one week away from the beginning of the summer recess, we're improvising a little bit, and rather than starting on a big subject that we won't be able to complete before the summer recess, I think we're going to try to move to some smaller areas that we can hopefully finish before the summer recess. So we're improvising, and I can assure you, Mr. President, there will be more binders to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're expecting them with baited breath. Thank you all, and we will resume Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
